e.etymology: A modern coinage in the Paisley and Kinsley family, joining Kai or Kay to the -slee ending.

e.meaning: part of Rudra, a form of Shiva
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Rudra, the fierce Vedic god identified with Shiva, and amsha, portion. It is a recent favorite in Hindu families.
A K spelling of Cleo, the short form of Cleopatra, from Greek kleos, glory.
A spelling of Kaylee, a late 20th-century name read as Kay plus Lee or as a form of the surnames Cayley and Keeley.
An older Spanish spelling of Alejandro and the form closest to Greek Alexandros, from alexein, to defend, and aner, man.
From Greek eulalos, sweetly speaking, from eu, well, and lalein, to talk. Early Spanish martyrs, among them Saint Eulalia of Barcelona, made it a favorite in Spain.
An anglicized form of Irish Caolán, from caol, slender, with a diminutive ending. Several early Irish saints bore the name.
The name of Princess Kitana in the Mortal Kombat fighting games, introduced in 1993. Its peak as a baby name came in 1996, the year after the first Mortal Kombat film.

assoc.t: sounds like katana, the Japanese sword

e.etymology: A modern American name in the sound family of Jabari, Jakari and Javon.
A feminine form of Evan, also read as a blend of Eva and Anna. Most people know it from Irish actress Evanna Lynch.
namesakes: Evanna Lynch (Luna Lovegood in the Harry Potter films)

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Job, from Hebrew Iyyov, the prophet whose patience under suffering is told in the Bible and the Quran. This French-style spelling is usual in North Africa and Lebanon.
A modern name, used mostly in Hispanic families in the US, in the sound family of Adalyn, Nataly and Magaly.
A modern American name that extends Ava with the -eah ending of Leah and Aleah.
From Arabic tahani, congratulations or good wishes. American use rose with Tahani Al-Jamil, a character on the sitcom The Good Place, which ran from 2016 to 2020.
namesakes: Tahani Al-Jamil (Jameela Jamil's character on The Good Place)

assoc.t: Tahani Al-Jamil of The Good Place

e.etymology: A respelling of Santiago, Spanish for Saint James, from santo and Yago, an old form of James. The th echoes Thiago, the Portuguese short form.
The Spanish and Portuguese feminine of Francisco, from Latin Franciscus, Frankish or French, the name that spread with Saint Francis of Assisi. Its English equivalents are Frances and Francesca.
A variant of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah, lily, a word that goes back to Egyptian for lotus. Susanna appears in the Bible's Apocrypha and in the Gospel of Luke.

e.meaning: of the Fabius family, from Latin faba, bean
e.etymology: A Latin diminutive of Fabia, the feminine of the Roman family name Fabius, from faba, bean. Saint Fabiola was a 4th-century Roman noblewoman who founded a hospital for the poor.
From the Irish surname Ó Brógáin, descendant of Brogan, a personal name that is probably a diminutive of brog, shoe.

assoc.t: brogan, a heavy ankle-high work boot

e.etymology: A spelling of Audrey, the medieval short form of Old English Aethelthryth, from aethel, noble, and thryth, strength. Saint Audrey was a 7th-century queen who founded Ely Abbey.
The Turkish form of Arabic Salim, safe or sound, from the root s-l-m that also gives salaam, peace. Three Ottoman sultans bore the name.
A modern blend of Wesley or Wes with Lynn. Wesley is an English surname meaning western meadow.
A rare spelling of Dale, the English word for a valley. In Spanish-speaking families it is a newer name said in two syllables, in the style of Yael and Abdiel.
A respelling of Hayes, a surname with Irish roots in Ó hAodha, descendant of Aodh, fire, and English roots in words for a hedged enclosure or brushwood. The spelling also evokes haze.

assoc.t: sounds like haze, mist or smog

e.etymology: A variant of Daleyza, a name that spread in Mexican American families after 2012, when singer Larry Hernández's daughter Daleyza appeared on the reality show Larrymania.
From the liquor, whose name shortens brandywine, from Dutch brandewijn, burnt wine. It caught on in 1970s America, helped by the 1972 hit song Brandy (You're a Fine Girl).
namesakes: Brandy Norwood (R&B singer and star of Moesha)

assoc.t: brandy, the liquor distilled from wine
Brandy, the R&B singer and actress
Brandy (You're a Fine Girl), 1972 hit song
Brandy Melville, teen clothing chain known as Brandy

e.note: Also the name of a liquor, which most people will notice.

e.etymology: A variant of Dylan, the name of a sea figure in Welsh legend, probably from dy-, great, and llanw, tide or flow. The -an spelling splits the difference with the Irish surname Dillon.
The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Linus, the name of the second pope, from Greek Linos, of uncertain meaning.
The French form of Oliver, first recorded in the 11th-century Song of Roland as the name of Roland's companion. It is traditionally tied to Latin oliva, olive tree.
From Arabic, either haris, guardian, or Harith, plowman or provider, in a spelling common in Bosnia and South Asia. Haris is also a Greek short form tied to charis, grace.
e.note: English speakers may read it as a misspelling of Harris.

e.etymology: The feminine of Avelino, given in honor of the 16th-century Italian saint Andrew Avellino, whose surname comes from the town of Avellino near Naples. It also serves as a Latin-style form of Aveline.
From Yiddish blum, flower, a traditional Ashkenazi girls' name also spelled Bluma. It is used mostly in Hasidic communities.
